## What this document is {.unnumbered}

This tutorial teaches **ggcarto**, an R package that brings cartographic color
scales and classification tools into ordinary ggplot2 workflows. But the goal
is not simply to learn a set of functions. The more important goal is to
understand the decisions those functions help you make.

A choropleth map looks simple: assign values to areas and fill the areas with
colors. In practice, every map requires a chain of substantive choices. Should
the variable be shown continuously or divided into classes? If it is classified,
where should the breaks go? How many distinctions can a reader realistically
use? Should the palette be sequential or diverging? What should happen to
outliers and missing values? If two variables appear on the same map, what can
the reader actually infer from the combined colors?

Those are not styling details. They determine which patterns become visible,
which differences are emphasized, and what claims a reader can reasonably make
from the map.

Every idea below is demonstrated with a real spatial dataset: the 217 counties
of the U.S. Northeast, from Pennsylvania to Maine. The discussion also connects
the software to the cartographic and perceptual research behind it. You should
be comfortable with basic R and ggplot2, but no prior cartography is assumed.

The package is organized around one sequence, and so is this tutorial:

> **inspect → choose → classify → map → diagnose**

Each step answers a different question:

- **Inspect:** What does the distribution actually look like?
- **Choose:** How much detail can the map support, and how much can the reader use?
- **Classify:** Where should the boundaries between groups fall?
- **Map:** How should those groups be encoded with color, labels, limits, and missing values?
- **Diagnose:** Does the finished map communicate the decisions you intended?

The recurring principle is simple: **understand the cartographic problem first;
choose the function second.**

## Setup

### Install

ggcarto lives on GitHub. The package builds on ggplot2 and classInt. In this
tutorial, **sf** supplies the county geometries, while the remaining packages
support layout, palettes, and tables. They are useful for the examples but are
not all required for every ggcarto workflow.

```{r}
#| label: install
#| eval: false
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jcapellan/ggcarto")
install.packages(c("sf", "dplyr", "patchwork", "RColorBrewer", "viridisLite",
                   "colorspace"))
```

```{r}
#| label: libraries
library(ggcarto)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
theme_set(theme_ggcarto(base_size = 12, legend = "right"))
```

### The data: counties of the Northeast

ggcarto ships `northeast_counties`, an **sf** object containing the 217 counties
in the Census Bureau's Northeast region and several variables from the
2015–2019 American Community Survey [@acs2019], compiled from the usdata package
[@usdata]. The object is already projected in an Albers equal-area conic
projection centered on the region, so `geom_sf()` can draw it directly.

The variables are intentionally different from one another. That matters
because there is no classification method that behaves well for every
distribution. A nearly symmetric unemployment rate, a strongly skewed
population count, and a variable with substantial missingness create different
cartographic problems—and should lead to different choices.

```{r}
#| label: data
data(northeast_counties)
cty <- northeast_counties
cty
```

The table below previews those differences:

| Variable | What it is | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| `unemployment` | unemployment rate, % | nearly symmetric — the easy case |
| `median_income` | median household income, $ | moderately right-skewed |
| `pop` | population | a heavy right tail: New York City's boroughs against rural Maine |
| `pct_bachelors` | adults with a bachelor's degree, % | wide, lumpy: metro against rural |
| `pct_poverty` | people below the poverty line, % | 49 counties missing |

```{r}
#| label: shapes
#| fig-height: 5
cty |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(unemployment, median_income, pop, pct_bachelors, pct_poverty) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free", ncol = 5) +
  theme_minimal(10) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank())
```

::: {.callout-note}
## sf is not required by ggcarto
Every scale in this document works identically with `geom_polygon()`,
`geom_tile()` or `geom_point()`. Nothing in ggcarto depends on the geometry
layer; sf is used here because it is what most people map with.
:::

`theme_ggcarto()` is the package's map theme — warm paper, a navy title,
grey annotation, no axes, the legend where a reader starts — and it is set as
the default above (`legend = "right"` here because the maps are wide; the
default puts it bottom-left). One helper, so that each map is one line and
side-by-side maps get a compact legend underneath:

```{r}
#| label: helper
ne_map <- function(var = "unemployment", data = cty, title = NULL) {
  ggplot(data) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[var]]), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    labs(title = title, fill = NULL) +
    theme(legend.key.height = unit(1.1, "lines"),
          plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
}

bottom_legend <- function(rows = 2) {
  list(theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
             legend.key.size = unit(0.9, "lines")),
       guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = rows, byrow = TRUE, reverse = TRUE)))
}
```

## The problem, in one picture

Before learning any functions, it helps to see the problem ggcarto is trying to
solve. Here is county unemployment drawn with ggplot2's default continuous
color scale:

```{r}
#| label: default
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map(title = "Unemployment rate: ggplot2 defaults")
```

The map is not statistically wrong. The problem is that it asks the reader to
do too much perceptual work. Try answering a simple question such as, "Which
counties are above 6%?" The continuous legend provides no explicit threshold,
nearby shades are difficult to distinguish, and the darkest color represents
the lowest values rather than the highest. The reader can sense a general
pattern, but it is surprisingly difficult to turn that impression into a clear
statement.

Now the same data with five classes, a palette made for maps, and labels that
read like sentences:

```{r}
#| label: fixed-classes
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map(title = "Unemployment rate: five classes") +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%",
                                          digits = 1, open = TRUE),
                       na.value = "grey85")
```

The second map is easier to read because several decisions have been made
explicit: the data are divided into five classes, the break locations are
chosen by a named method, the palette has an ordered light-to-dark structure,
and the legend translates the numerical breaks into readable ranges.

Everything that follows is about understanding those decisions. **How many
classes? Where should the breaks go? Which palette matches the meaning of the
variable? How should the legend describe the classes? What happens to missing
or extreme values?** These choices are part of the analysis, not decoration.

## Why maps are not charts

### Color is a relatively weak quantitative channel

A scatterplot encodes numbers primarily through *position*. That is useful
because people are very good at comparing positions along a common scale. In
Cleveland and McGill's experiments, position was among the most accurately
decoded visual channels, while color saturation and shading performed much
worse [@cleveland1984]. Bertin reached a related conclusion from cartographic
design: among the visual variables available to maps, lightness can express
order, but only a limited number of steps remain easy to distinguish
[@bertin1983].

A choropleth map faces a special constraint. Geographic position is already
being used to show *where* a county is, so color has to carry most of the
quantitative information. The reader therefore has to infer numerical order
from a visual channel that is less precise than position.

That does not make choropleth maps bad. It means they work best when the map
asks color to communicate **a manageable number of meaningful distinctions**
rather than pretending that readers can recover exact values from dozens of
slightly different shades.

### Classification makes many map questions easier to answer

Classification is a form of **purposeful simplification**. A continuous ramp
preserves more numerical detail, but much of that detail cannot be reliably
read from color alone. Dividing the data into a small number of classes throws
away some precision in exchange for clearer comparisons. Instead of asking the
reader to distinguish 5.8% from 6.1% by shade, the map can ask a simpler
question: are both counties in the same range, or does one cross a meaningful
boundary?

That trade-off is why cartographic texts often recommend roughly five to seven
classes for ordinary choropleth maps [@slocum2009; @dent2009; @brewer2016]. It
is a guideline, not a law. Fewer classes emphasize broad regional structure;
more classes preserve more variation but place greater demands on the reader.
With a diverging scheme, an odd number of classes is often useful when you want
a true neutral middle class; an even number can be preferable when the
meaningful midpoint should be a boundary between classes.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When *not* to classify
Classification is useful when readers need distinct, interpretable groups. A
continuous ramp can be better when the phenomenon itself is continuous, when
smooth gradients matter more than thresholds, when exact values are available
interactively on hover, or when classification would create artificial
boundaries that are not substantively meaningful. Elevation and other
continuous surfaces are common examples.

The question is not "classified or continuous—which is correct?" It is **which
representation better serves the task the reader needs to perform?** ggcarto's
`scale_fill_cont()` supports the continuous case.
:::

### Why the breaks matter so much

Classification is lossy: values inside the same class are treated as visually
equivalent. Where the breaks fall therefore determines which differences are
preserved and which are deliberately suppressed. Here are four maps of the
same variable with the same number of classes and the same palette. Only the
classification method changes.

```{r}
#| label: four-methods
#| fig-height: 8
methods <- c("equal", "quantile", "fisher", "sd")
maps4 <- lapply(methods, function(st) {
  ne_map("pct_bachelors", title = paste0('style = "', st, '"')) +
    scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = st, n = 5,
                         labels = label_map(style = "interval", digits = 0,
                                            open = TRUE, suffix = "%")) +
    bottom_legend()
})
wrap_plots(maps4, ncol = 2)
```

Four honest maps, four different stories. Equal intervals says most of the
Northeast is in the middle and only a ring of suburban counties stands out.
Quantiles say the Boston–New York–Philadelphia corridor is one thing and
everything else is another. Fisher's natural breaks land in between. Standard
deviations center the story on "above or below the regional average".

So the classification is an *argument*, not a setting, and you should be able
to say which question your map answers [@monmonier2018]:

| The question the map answers | Method that fits |
|---|---|
| Where are the high (or low) values? | natural breaks (`fisher`, `jenks`) |
| How is this spread across the region? Which counties are in the top fifth? | `quantile` |
| Which counties are above the average, and by how much? | `sd` |
| Is this above the policy threshold? | fixed breaks you choose |
| How does this year compare with last year? | the *same* fixed breaks both years |
| Where are the extreme cases in a heavy-tailed variable? | `headtails`, `log` |

## Inspect: understand the distribution before choosing breaks

Classification should begin with the distribution, not with a favorite GIS
default. The same method can work beautifully on one variable and badly on
another because classification methods respond differently to skew, gaps,
outliers, and repeated values.

The purpose of the **inspect** step is therefore diagnostic: learn what the data
look like before deciding how the map should simplify them.

### What a break actually does

A class interval method takes a numeric variable and returns `n + 1` cut points
that divide it into `n` classes. Those cut points are not merely legend labels.
They determine which observations the map treats as similar and where it draws
a visual boundary between them.

In ggcarto, `compute_breaks()` lets you inspect those boundaries directly:

```{r}
#| label: compute-breaks
compute_breaks(cty$unemployment, style = "quantile", n = 5)
compute_breaks(cty$unemployment, style = "fisher",   n = 5)
compute_breaks(cty$unemployment, style = "equal",    n = 5)
```

Every style is also available as a *factory* — `breaks_quantile(5)` returns a
function that computes those breaks from whatever data it is given — so a style
can be handed to a scale and evaluated later, when the scale finally sees the
data:

```{r}
#| label: factories
f <- breaks_jenks(6)
f
f(cty$unemployment)
```

`map_styles_info()` is the in-package cheat sheet:

```{r}
#| label: styles-info
knitr::kable(map_styles_info())
```

### See the method before you trust it

A list of break values is useful, but it is much easier to understand a
classification method when you can see where those breaks fall on the actual
distribution. `plot_breaks()` overlays one method on a histogram;
`compare_breaks()` places several methods over the same data and shows how many
observations each class contains.

This is an important habit: **inspect the classification before mapping it.** A
method can have a sensible name and still produce a poor set of classes for the
variable in front of you.

```{r}
#| label: compare-breaks-unemp
#| fig-height: 8
compare_breaks(cty$unemployment,
               c("equal", "pretty", "quantile", "fisher", "sd", "headtails"),
               n = 5)
```

Read the panels as competing answers to the same question: *which differences
in this distribution should the map make visually important?*

**Equal interval** (`equal`) slices the *range* into equal widths. It is honest
about magnitude — one step in color is one step in value — and it is what a
reader assumes a legend means unless told otherwise. On a nearly symmetric
variable like this one it works; on a skewed one it does not, as the
population section shows. `pretty` is the same idea with the cut points rounded
to numbers people can read (4, 6, 8 ...), which is why it is ggplot2's own
default for binned scales.

**Quantile** (`quantile`) puts equal *counts* in each class. Every class is
populated, the map is visually balanced, and the legend can be read as "top
fifth of counties". The cost is that class widths become unequal and the map
hides that. In Brewer and Pickle's map-reading experiment with 56 subjects and
nine series of US mortality maps, quantiles nonetheless produced the most
accurate answers to general map-reading questions, and "the advantages of
careful optimization procedures in choropleth classification seem to offer no
benefit over the simpler quantile method" [@brewer2002].

**Natural breaks** (`fisher`, `jenks`, and the clustering variants `kmeans`,
`hclust`, `bclust`) look for gaps in the data. Formally they choose breaks that
minimize the variance *within* classes and maximize it *between* them
[@jenks1967; @jenks1971]. `fisher` is Walter Fisher's exact dynamic-programming
solution to that problem [@fisher1958]; `jenks` is George Jenks's iterative
approximation of it, the one built into GIS software. They give near-identical
results; `fisher` is faster and is the one to use. Natural breaks follow the
data's own structure, which makes them a useful starting point for a single
descriptive map. The two costs are that the cut points can look arbitrary
(4.3%, 5.1%) and are specific to *this* dataset, so independently classified
maps are not directly comparable [@coulson1987; @evans1977].

**Standard deviation** (`sd`) puts the breaks at the mean and at ±1, ±2 ... SD
from it. Use it when the question is "above or below average, and by how
much", and pair it with a diverging palette so the mean is the neutral color.
It only makes sense for roughly symmetric data — which unemployment is.

**Head/tail breaks** (`headtails`) are designed for heavy-tailed variables—
population, income, or other measures in which a small number of areas are much
larger than the rest [@jiang2013]. The method splits at the mean, keeps the
values above the mean (the "head"), then repeats the process within that head.
It chooses its own class count. On a roughly symmetric variable it stops early,
which is useful diagnostic information: the distribution does not have the
recursive heavy-tail structure the method is designed to reveal.

Three more, for completeness: `box` uses the quartiles and the 1.5·IQR
fences from a boxplot, so outliers get their own classes; `dpih` uses
kernel-density bandwidth selection to choose histogram bins [@wand1997];
`maximum` splits at the widest empty gaps in the sorted values. All of these
except `equal`, `pretty`, `quantile`, `sd`, `log`, `geometric` and `unique` are
computed by the **classInt** package [@classint], which is the reference
implementation in R.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exact, and the same every time
classInt takes a shortcut on large vectors: above 3,000 values it computes
`fisher` and `jenks` on a random 10% sample, and the sample is drawn from the
session's random number generator, so a map of the 3,100 US counties could
class differently every time it was drawn. ggcarto turns that off. Fisher is
computed exactly at any size (about 0.3 s for 10,000 values), and every style
with a random component (`kmeans`, `bclust`) is seeded. `?compute_breaks`
documents the details and the `large_n` argument that restores the shortcut,
reproducibly, if you need it.
:::

### Heavy tails: population

County population is a classic heavy-tailed variable: the median county in the
region has about 100,000 residents, while Kings County (Brooklyn) has roughly
2.6 million. This is exactly the kind of distribution for which a method that
works well on unemployment can become misleading. Compare how equal intervals,
quantiles, and tail-aware approaches allocate the same observations:

```{r}
#| label: compare-breaks-pop
#| fig-height: 8
compare_breaks(cty$pop, c("equal", "quantile", "fisher", "headtails", "log", "geometric"),
               n = 5, log_x = TRUE)
```

On a log axis the equal-interval breaks all pile up at the right — four of the
five classes hold a handful of counties between them. `log` puts breaks at 1,
2, 5 per decade; `geometric` uses a constant ratio between breaks; `headtails`
stops when the tail stops. On the map:

```{r}
#| label: pop-maps
#| fig-height: 4.6
p1 <- ne_map("pop", title = 'style = "equal" (poor fit)') +
  scale_fill_intervals("viridis::mako", style = "equal", n = 5, reverse = TRUE,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", big.mark = ",")) +
  bottom_legend(3)
p2 <- ne_map("pop", title = 'style = "log"') +
  scale_fill_intervals("viridis::mako", style = "log", n = 6, reverse = TRUE,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", big.mark = ",")) +
  bottom_legend(3)
p1 | p2
```

## Choose: decide how much detail the map can support

After choosing a classification family, the next question is how many classes
to show. There is no universally optimal answer because the choice balances two
competing goals: preserving meaningful variation in the data and keeping the
map readable.

`class_guide()` makes that trade-off visible. For each candidate class count it
summarizes four considerations:

| Consideration | The practical question |
|---|---|
| **Fit** | How much of the original variation is preserved by the classes? |
| **Balance** | Does each color represent enough observations to be useful? |
| **Separation** | Are adjacent break values meaningfully different, or are we drawing distinctions the data barely support? |
| **Perception** | Are there so many ordered colors that readers will struggle to distinguish and remember them? |

The function then applies explicit, method-specific rules to make a
**suggestion**. That wording matters. `class_guide()` can evaluate statistical
and perceptual trade-offs, but it cannot know the substantive purpose of your
map.

```{r}
#| label: class-guide
g <- class_guide(cty$pct_bachelors, style = "fisher")
g
```

For natural-break methods, *fit* is summarized with the goodness of variance
fit, $1 - SSW/SST$, proposed by Jenks and Caspall for evaluating choropleth
classifications [@jenks1971]. A value near 1 means the classes capture most of
the variation between observations; a smaller value means substantial
variation remains hidden within classes.

The recommendation then looks for a point of diminishing returns: a class count
with good fit, little improvement from adding another class, no nearly empty
classes, and no unnecessary perceptual burden. The exact thresholds are stated
in `?class_guide`; `summary()` and `plot()` expose the evidence behind the
suggestion so the rule never has to be taken on faith.

```{r}
#| label: class-guide-plot
#| fig-height: 5
plot(g)
```

```{r}
#| label: class-guide-balance
#| fig-height: 4
plot(g, type = "balance")
```

The rules are method-specific because the methods are. For `quantile` the
classes are balanced by construction, so fit is beside the point; the guide
instead checks whether adding classes forces breaks so close together that the
legend draws distinctions the data cannot support. For `equal` it counts the
classes the skew has emptied. For `headtails` it reports the count the method
chose and why, because `n` is not part of that method. For `fixed` it declines
to recommend anything: the thresholds are yours.

```{r}
#| label: class-guide-others
class_guide(cty$pop, style = "equal")
class_guide(cty$pop, style = "headtails")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## A suggestion, not an answer
`class_guide()` encodes the conventional trade-offs and shows its working. It
does not know what your map is *for*. If the policy threshold is 10%, use a
break at 10%. If the map will sit next to last year's, use last year's breaks.
The guide is where to start the argument, not where to end it.
:::

## Classify: turn the distribution into explicit groups

Suppose the guide suggests four classes for the share of college graduates but
shows five as a defensible alternative. If the purpose of the map is to reveal
a finer rural-to-metropolitan gradient, the fifth class may be worth the extra
legend entry. That is precisely the kind of judgment the software should
inform rather than make for you.

Once you have chosen a method and a class count, `class_summary()` shows the
classification as a table: each class's bounds, the label that will appear in
the legend, and the number of counties assigned to it. Because it uses the same
break engine as the plotting scales, the table is a direct audit of what the
map will display.

```{r}
#| label: class-summary
class_summary(cty$pct_bachelors, "fisher", 5)
```

And `plot_breaks()` puts those classes on the histogram:

```{r}
#| label: plot-breaks
#| fig-height: 3.4
plot_breaks(cty$pct_bachelors, "fisher", 5)
```

### Where does a value *on* the break go?

A value of exactly 30 with a break at 30 has to go somewhere. ggplot2's binned
scales put it in the class *below* — the classes are `(a, b]` — and so does
ggcarto by default. classInt and tmap default to the other convention,
`[a, b)`. It rarely matters for continuous rates; it matters a great deal for
integer data and for policy thresholds, where "10 and above" should mean what
it says. The `closure` argument makes the choice explicit, and `class_summary()`
shows the consequence:

```{r}
#| label: closure
x <- c(1, 5, 10, 10, 10, 15, 20)
class_summary(x, breaks = c(0, 10, 20), closure = "right")$n   # 10 goes below
class_summary(x, breaks = c(0, 10, 20), closure = "left")$n    # 10 goes above
```

For counts — 0, 1, 2, 3 ... — `as_count = TRUE` goes further: breaks are
rounded to whole numbers, classes are left-closed, and the labels read the way
a count legend should, "0 to 4", "5 to 9", never "0 to 5", "5 to 10":

```{r}
#| label: as-count
set.seed(1)
k <- rpois(300, 3)
class_summary(k, "quantile", 4, as_count = TRUE)
```

### Fixed breaks: when comparability matters more than local fit

Data-driven breaks are useful for describing one distribution well. They are
usually the wrong choice when the reader must compare multiple maps. If each
year, state, or outcome gets its own natural breaks, the same color can mean a
different numerical range from one panel to the next. Apparent visual change
may then reflect changing break points rather than changing data.

For map series, use the **same fixed breaks** across panels whenever direct
comparison is the goal. Brewer and Pickle found that matched legends improved
map-comparison accuracy substantially in their experiment [@brewer2002]. Fixed
breaks are also appropriate when the thresholds already have substantive
meaning—a poverty benchmark, a regulatory cutoff, a target, or a round number
that readers are expected to remember.

Both cases are `breaks =`:

```{r}
#| label: fixed-breaks
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map(title = "Unemployment rate: round-number breaks") +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", breaks = c(0, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%",
                                          open = TRUE),
                       na.value = "grey85")
```

A useful workflow for a one-off descriptive map is to use `class_guide()` and
`class_summary()` with `fisher` to see where the distribution naturally
separates, then consider whether nearby round-number thresholds communicate the
same pattern more clearly. Do not round mechanically: if moving a break changes
the substantive grouping, keep the data-driven break or choose a threshold with
a defensible external meaning.

### Why ggcarto needs its own ggplot2 scale machinery

ggplot2 has a binned scale, `scale_fill_binned()`, and it accepts a `breaks`
function. So you would expect this to give quantile classes:

```{r}
#| label: trap
p <- ggplot(cty, aes(pct_bachelors, median_income, colour = unemployment)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_binned(breaks = breaks_quantile(5))
b <- ggplot_build(p)
b$plot$scales$get_scales("colour")$get_breaks()
compute_breaks(cty$unemployment, "quantile", 5)
```

It does not. ggplot2 calls a binned scale's `breaks` function with the scale
*limits* — two numbers, the minimum and maximum — not with the data. Given two
numbers, every data-driven algorithm collapses to equal intervals, and nothing
warns you. The same trap catches a function passed as `limits`: it, too, sees
only the two endpoints, so a quantile-based trim would trim the wrong thing.
ggcarto's scales are built on small ggplot2 subclasses that keep the trained
values and hand the break and limit functions the real distribution. That one
fix is the reason the package exists; the rest is ergonomics around it.

## Map: make the cartographic choices explicit

By this stage, the classification itself should be defensible. The remaining
choices determine how faithfully that classification reaches the reader. These
are the details that often look cosmetic in code—limits, midpoint, missing-data
color, legend wording—but they carry substantive meaning on a map.

### Outliers: show them as extreme, not missing

ggplot2's continuous scales, when given `limits`, turn any value outside them
into `NA` and draw it in the missing-value color. On a map that is the wrong
message: a county with an extreme value is not a county with no data. The
cartographic convention is to *clamp* — outliers get the color of the end
class and the legend says "$110,000 and above". ggcarto's scales default to
`oob = "squish"` for this reason, and `trim_limits()` gives you a principled
way to choose limits that leave the outliers out of the ramp without dropping
them from the map:

```{r}
#| label: squish
#| fig-height: 4.2
p1 <- ne_map("median_income", title = "limits = full range") +
  scale_fill_cont("viridis::inferno", reverse = TRUE,
                  labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k"))
p2 <- ne_map("median_income", title = "limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.98), oob = squish") +
  scale_fill_cont("viridis::inferno", reverse = TRUE,
                  limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.98),
                  labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k"))
(p1 | p2) & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The left map spends the top of its ramp on the four suburban counties above
$100,000, so the other 213 are squeezed into the lower colors. The right map
gives the ramp to the bulk of the data and clamps the extremes — and its
legend says so. A ggcarto colourbar whose limits have squished data labels
the limit ticks "$41k or less" and "$107k and above", because `label_map()`
defaults to `open = "auto"`: an end opens exactly when there are values
beyond it. `guide_map()` draws the bar at a readable length, framed and
ticked, so the ends read as edges:

```{r}
#| label: squish-legend
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map("median_income", title = "Median household income, top and bottom 2% clamped") +
  scale_fill_cont("viridis::inferno", reverse = TRUE,
                  limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.98),
                  labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k", digits = 0),
                  guide = guide_map()) +
  theme_ggcarto()
```

### Diverging data: make the meaningful midpoint visually neutral

A diverging palette has two hues meeting at a neutral color. It is the right
choice only when the data have a *meaningful middle* — zero change, the
regional average, 50% of the vote — and the neutral color must sit exactly on
that value [@brewer1994]. Two things go wrong otherwise: the palette's midpoint
drifts to the middle of the data range, and unequal ranges either side make one
hue look more intense than the other for the same distance from the middle.

`midpoint =` fixes the first; `symmetric_limits()` fixes the second. With
classed data, `midpoint` also nudges a class break to sit exactly on it, so the
neutral color is a class boundary rather than the middle of a class.

```{r}
#| label: diverging
#| fig-height: 4.2
regional <- weighted.mean(cty$unemployment, cty$pop)
p1 <- ne_map(title = "Unemployment: no anchor") +
  scale_fill_cont("brewer::RdBu", reverse = TRUE)
p2 <- ne_map(title = sprintf("midpoint = regional rate (%.1f%%), symmetric limits", regional)) +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", reverse = TRUE, n = 6,
                       midpoint = regional, limits = symmetric_limits(regional),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%",
                                          digits = 1)) +
  bottom_legend()
(p1 | p2) & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

On the left, the neutral color lands at about 5.6% — the middle of the data
range — so a county with the regional rate reads as "better than average". On
the right, white is the regional rate and the reds and blues are equal
distances from it.

`midpoint` alone still lets the classification method decide how many
classes fall on each side, and a method that follows the data will give the
long side more of them. `mirror` builds the classes symmetrically about the
midpoint instead: `mirror = "value"` finds `n` breaks on the *distances* from
the midpoint and reflects them, so equal color steps mean equal data
distances on both sides; `mirror = "count"` classifies each side separately,
the quantile answer. Either way `n` is classes *per side*, the whole
symmetric set is kept even where one side's data stop short — so the
palette's neutral color stays on the midpoint — and `center = "band"` turns
the middle break into a neutral class. The legend opens both ends
automatically.

```{r}
#| label: mirror
#| fig-height: 4.6
gap <- cty$unemployment - regional
cty$unemp_gap <- gap
class_summary(gap, "pretty", n = 3, midpoint = 0, mirror = "value",
              labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = " pts", digits = 1))
ne_map("unemp_gap", title = "Unemployment relative to the regional rate: 3 classes per side") +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", reverse = TRUE, style = "pretty", n = 3,
                       midpoint = 0, mirror = "value",
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = " pts", digits = 1),
                       guide = guide_map("keys", direction = "vertical"))
```

The lowest class — more than three points *below* the regional rate — has
no county in it, and `diagnose_map()` will say so; it is kept so that the
deepest blue and the deepest red mean the same distance from the middle.

### Missing data must look different from low values

An area with no data should be a neutral color that cannot be mistaken for a
low value, and the legend should say so [@brewer2016]. `na.value` sets the
color. For categorical and ordinal scales ggplot2 draws the key itself and
`na.label` names it. Its binned and continuous legends have no slot for an NA
key, so for interval and continuous scales add `na_key()` to the plot; it
draws a filled square under the main legend and nothing on the map. Poverty is
missing for 49 of the 217 counties, which is what a real map looks like:

```{r}
#| label: missing
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map("pct_poverty", title = "Poverty rate: the missing counties have a legend entry") +
  scale_fill_intervals("hcl::Batlow", style = "quantile", n = 5, na.value = "grey85",
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", digits = 1, suffix = "%")) +
  na_key("No data (49 counties)", fill = "grey85")
```

### Write legend labels for readers, not for the computer

`label_map()` returns a labeling function. `style = "interval"` turns `n + 1`
break points into `n` range labels; `open` writes the first and last as
"Under x" and "x and above" rather than showing the data extremes — `TRUE`
always, `"auto"` (the default) only where the scale has squished values past
a limit, so the legend is honest without being asked; `prefix`, `suffix`,
`big.mark` and `digits` do what they say. It works in any ggplot2 scale, not
only ggcarto's (outside a ggcarto scale, `"auto"` is closed, since nothing
is known about the data).

```{r}
#| label: labels
label_map(suffix = "%", digits = 0)(c(2.5, 7.5, 12.5))
label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%", digits = 0)(c(0, 5, 10, 31))
label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%", digits = 0, open = TRUE)(c(0, 5, 10, 31))
label_map(prefix = "$", big.mark = ",", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k")(c(12500, 48000))
```

Two conventions are especially useful. First, round labels to a precision that
matches the claim the map can support; most readers do not benefit from a class
boundary such as 12.93% [@brewer2016]. Second, when the observed minimum and
maximum have no substantive meaning, use open-ended classes. "Under 5%" states
a reusable threshold; "1.2% to 5%" merely reports the minimum happened to be
1.2% in this dataset.

## Color: match the palette to the meaning of the data

A palette is not simply a set of attractive colors. Its visual structure should
match the logical structure of the variable. A reader should be able to infer
"more," "less," "different," or "above versus below" from the palette before
reading every legend label.

### Three kinds of palette

Brewer's color-use guidelines, the basis of ColorBrewer, sort palettes by the
kind of data they encode [@brewer1994; @harrower2003]:

* **Sequential** — one hue, light to dark, for ordered data with a low and a
  high. The lightness ramp does the work; hue is decoration.
* **Diverging** — two hues meeting at a neutral, for ordered data with a
  meaningful middle. (See the unemployment map above.)
* **Qualitative** — distinct hues at similar lightness, for categories with
  no order. Never for a number.

Ordered categories ("low / medium / high," or classes from an interval scale)
need a *sequential* palette, not a qualitative one. Rainbow palettes are poor
choices for ordered data because their lightness does not progress consistently:
they can create apparent boundaries where the data have none and weaken real
ones. They can also become difficult to interpret under common forms of
color-vision deficiency [@borland2007; @crameri2020].

```{r}
#| label: palette-kinds
#| fig-height: 2.6
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
show_palette("brewer::YlGnBu", 7)
show_palette("brewer::RdBu", 7)
show_palette("brewer::Set2", 7)
par(op)
```

### Checking a palette

Palettes fail in predictable ways: the palest class vanishes against a white
page; two adjacent classes are too close to separate on small polygons; a
red–green scheme collapses for a color-blind reader; a "diverging" palette has
no neutral center. `check_palette()` measures those things — CIELAB lightness
and color difference, contrast against the background, and color-vision
simulation via the colorspace package [@zeileis2020] — and says what each one
would do to the map:

```{r}
#| label: check-palette
check_palette("brewer::YlGnBu", 5)
check_palette("brewer::RdYlGn", 7)
```

`plot_palette()` simulates how the classes appear under common forms of
color-vision deficiency. Look for adjacent classes whose boundary becomes weak
or disappears in one of the simulated rows:

```{r}
#| label: plot-palette
#| fig-height: 3.6
plot_palette("brewer::RdYlGn", 7)
```

### Where good palettes come from

Nobody needs to design a palette from scratch. Several R packages carry
palettes that have been designed and tested, and they differ in what they are
for:

| Source | Prefix in ggcarto | Roughly how many | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| grDevices `hcl.colors()` | `hcl::` | 115 | Palettes built in perceptual HCL space, shipped with R itself; no dependency [@zeileis2020] |
| RColorBrewer | `brewer::` | 35 | Cynthia Brewer's ColorBrewer schemes, designed for maps, tested for color-blind safety and print [@harrower2003; @rcolorbrewer] |
| viridisLite | `viridis::` | 8 | viridis, magma, plasma, inferno, cividis, mako, rocket, turbo: perceptually uniform, color-blind safe [@smith2015; @viridislite] |
| cols4all | `c4a::` | ~700 | The palette library behind tmap, each scored for color-blind friendliness and contrast [@cols4all] |
| paletteer | any `package::name` | ~2,500 | An index of palettes from dozens of other packages (scico, rcartocolor, MetBrewer, wesanderson ...) [@paletteer] |

ggcarto does not carry palettes of its own. `as_palette()` resolves any of the
above through one `"source::name"` syntax and returns a function of `n`:

```{r}
#| label: as-palette
as_palette("brewer::YlGnBu")(5)
as_palette("hcl::Zissou 1", reverse = TRUE)(5)
as_palette(c("#f7fbff", "#08306b"))(5)      # your own colours, interpolated
palette_sources()                            # which sources are installed
```

`map_palettes()` searches them:

```{r}
#| label: map-palettes
map_palettes("div", source = "brewer")
head(map_palettes(pattern = "blue"))
```

### Three palette tricks

**Trim the washed-out end.** The lightest color of most sequential ramps is
nearly white and vanishes against a white page or a white county border.
`range = c(0.15, 1)` drops it — `check_palette()` will tell you when you need
to.

**Reverse when the ramp runs the wrong way.** Dark should mean *more* of
whatever the map is about. Several viridis palettes are light-at-the-top;
`reverse = TRUE`.

**Even or by value.** With classed data, `interpolate = "even"` (the default)
gives each class an evenly spaced color from the ramp — what GIS software and
tmap do, and what makes classes distinguishable. `interpolate = "value"` places
each class's color at its position along the data range, so a wide class sits
further along the ramp; it is more faithful to magnitude and less legible.

```{r}
#| label: palette-tricks
#| fig-height: 4.2
p1 <- ne_map("median_income", title = 'range = c(0, 1): first class is white') +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::Blues", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                          scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k", digits = 0)) +
  bottom_legend()
p2 <- ne_map("median_income", title = 'range = c(0.2, 1)') +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::Blues", style = "fisher", n = 5, range = c(0.2, 1),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                          scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k", digits = 0)) +
  bottom_legend()
p1 | p2
```

## Diagnose: audit the finished map

A map can look polished and still contain choices that work against its
message. The finished figure does not tell you that the top class contains only
six counties, that 4% of the observations were clamped into the end classes,
that a diverging midpoint falls outside the data, or that the missing-data gray
is nearly indistinguishable from one of the substantive classes.

`diagnose_map()` turns the final map back into a set of inspectable decisions.
It finds the ggcarto scale and the variable behind it, then reports the
classification, class counts, limits, midpoint behavior, out-of-bounds handling,
and palette concerns. The point is quality control: **after making the map, ask
whether a reasonable reader will see what you intended them to see.**

Its warnings are therefore written in terms of likely reading consequences,
not as declarations that a map is "wrong":

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think of `diagnose_map()` as a unit test for cartography
The function does not decide whether your substantive choices are correct. It
checks whether the finished scale behaves consistently with those choices. A
warning is a prompt to inspect the map, not an instruction to change it.
:::

```{r}
#| label: diagnose
final <- ne_map("median_income", title = "Median household income") +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       range = c(0.15, 1), na.value = "grey85",
                       limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.98),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                          big.mark = ",", digits = 0, open = TRUE))
diagnose_map(final)
```

```{r}
#| label: final-map
#| fig-height: 5
final
```

The same diagnosis is available before you build anything, from a scale and a
vector: `diagnose_scale(scale_fill_intervals(...), cty$median_income)`. Here is
what it says about a map that gets three things wrong at once — a diverging
palette with no midpoint, too many classes, and a missing-data color that
looks like a class:

```{r}
#| label: diagnose-bad
diagnose_scale(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", "quantile", n = 8,
                                    na.value = "#d1e5f0"),
               cty$pct_poverty)$warnings
```

## One engine, five ways to interpret a variable

Everything so far has used `scale_fill_intervals()`, but classification is only
one way to translate a variable into color. ggcarto treats the *mapping type*
as an explicit analytical choice. All five types below are handled by the same
`scale_map()` engine; changing `type` changes the interpretation without forcing
you to rebuild the rest of the scale call.

This design follows an idea also emphasized by tmap [@tennekes2018]: the first
question should be **what kind of relationship between values and colors do I
want?** Only then should you worry about the exact syntax.

| `type` | What it does | Shorthand |
|---|---|---|
| `"continuous"` | smooth ramp | `scale_fill_cont()` |
| `"intervals"` | classed into `n` bins by `style` | `scale_fill_intervals()` |
| `"categorical"` | unordered categories, qualitative palette | `scale_fill_cat()` |
| `"ordinal"` | ordered categories, sequential palette | `scale_fill_ord()` |
| `"rank"` | color by position in the distribution | `scale_fill_rank()` |

`palette`, `limits`, `oob`, `reverse`, `range`, `na.value`, `labels`
and `name` mean the same thing in all five.

```{r}
#| label: five-types
#| fig-height: 10
cty$income_ord <- cut(cty$median_income, c(0, 50000, 65000, 85000, Inf),
                      labels = c("Under $50k", "$50k to $65k", "$65k to $85k", "$85k and above"))
maps5 <- list(
  ne_map("median_income", title = "continuous") +
    scale_fill_map("hcl::Batlow", type = "continuous",
                   labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k")),
  ne_map("median_income", title = "intervals") +
    scale_fill_map("hcl::Batlow", type = "intervals", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                   labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                      scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k", digits = 0)) +
    bottom_legend(),
  ne_map("income_ord", title = "ordinal") +
    scale_fill_map("hcl::Batlow", type = "ordinal") + bottom_legend(1),
  ne_map("state", title = "categorical") +
    scale_fill_map("brewer::Set3", type = "categorical") + bottom_legend(2),
  ne_map("median_income", title = "rank") +
    scale_fill_map("hcl::Batlow", type = "rank",
                   labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k")) +
    bottom_legend(1)
)
wrap_plots(maps5, ncol = 2) & theme(legend.position = "bottom",
                                     legend.text = element_text(size = 8))
```

The **rank** type deserves a word. It colors each county by its relative
position in the distribution: the median county receives the middle color
regardless of the raw value. Because color is assigned by rank rather than
absolute distance, the visual allocation is much less sensitive to skew and
extreme values. Conceptually, it is similar to a quantile classification with
as many levels as there are distinct ranks. Its legend keys are therefore
placed at data quantiles; evenly spaced *value* ticks would misrepresent how
the color ramp is being used.

## Two variables on one map: bivariate choropleths

### Use them to study a relationship, not to save space

A bivariate choropleth assigns each area a color based on **two variables at
once**. Each variable is divided into `n` classes, creating `n × n` possible
combinations, and each combination receives one color from an `n × n` grid.
The technique dates to Judy Olson's work at the Census Bureau in the 1970s
[@olson1975]; the now-familiar 3 × 3 form combines two ordered color ramps so
that the legend can be read in two directions [@stevens2015; @leonowicz2006].

The crucial question is *why* you are using one. A bivariate map is not simply a
way to put two variables into one figure. Its purpose is to reveal their
**spatial relationship**: places where both are high, both are low, or where
one is high and the other is low. In that sense, the most interesting areas are
often the off-diagonal exceptions.

The trade-off is cognitive load. The reader must decode a two-dimensional
legend and match combined colors back to it. That is why 3 × 3 is the standard
starting point; 4 × 4 can work with a carefully designed legend, while larger
grids quickly become difficult to use [@stevens2015]. If your real question is
simply "Where is variable X high?", use a univariate map instead.

### Palette

ggcarto ships two kinds of preset. *Corner* palettes are defined by four
colors — both low (near white), `x` high, `y` high, both high (dark) — and
filled in between, so they work at any `n`. *Grid* palettes are the complete
3 × 3 schemes Joshua Stevens published for bivariate maps [@stevens2015],
the ones the biscale package popularised (`"stevens-purpleblue"` and
friends), resampled when `n` is not 3. You can also pass four corner colors
of your own, a full `k × k` grid of colors, two sequential ramps to multiply
the way a printer overlays inks, or, with cols4all installed, one of its
bivariate palettes as `"c4a::<name>"`.

```{r}
#| label: bipal
bivariate_palette("blue-red", n = 3)
names(bivariate_palettes())
```

```{r}
#| label: bipal-all
#| fig-height: 6
plot_bivariate_palettes()
```

```{r}
#| label: bipal-gallery
#| fig-height: 2.6
wrap_plots(
  legend_bivariate("blue-red", 3, "x", "y", text_size = 8),
  legend_bivariate("purple-green", 3, "x", "y", text_size = 8),
  legend_bivariate(c("#f3f3f3", "steelblue", "firebrick", "#2b1b2b"), 4,
                   "x", "y", text_size = 8),
  legend_bivariate(list(x = "brewer::Blues", y = "brewer::Reds"), 3,
                   "x", "y", text_size = 8),
  nrow = 1
)
```

### Building the map: classify, color, then explain the combination

A bivariate map has three linked pieces: classification, color, and a
purpose-built legend. If any one of the three is unclear, the map becomes hard
to interpret.

First, classify both variables into one joint factor. Quantile breaks are a
common starting point because they keep observations distributed across each
variable's classes, which helps avoid entire empty rows or columns in the
legend. That is a practical reason, not a universal rule; substantively
meaningful fixed thresholds may be better when the variables have known
benchmarks.

Income is skewed here, so it is classified on a log scale. `trans_x = "log10"`
changes the scale on which the breaks are found, while still reporting the
resulting break values in dollars. The reader therefore gets a familiar legend
without you having to back-transform labels manually.

```{r}
#| label: bi-classify
cty$bi <- classify_bivariate(cty$median_income, cty$pct_bachelors, n = 3,
                             style_x = "quantile", style_y = "quantile",
                             trans_x = "log10")
table(cty$bi)
attr(cty$bi, "breaks_x")
attr(cty$bi, "breaks_y")
```

Second, color the map. `scale_fill_bivariate()` keeps all nine classes even if
one is empty, so map and legend always agree, and it draws no legend of its
own.

Third, the legend. A ggplot2 legend is a column of keys; a bivariate legend has
to be a grid, so `legend_bivariate()` draws it as a small ggplot and
`inset_legend()` places it on the map. Passing `classes =` hands it the break
points — already in the original units; `ends = FALSE` labels only the
interior cut points, which is cleaner.

```{r}
#| label: bi-map
#| fig-height: 6
bimap <- ggplot(cty) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = bi), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_bivariate("purple-green", n = 3) +
  labs(title = "Income and education, Northeast counties") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"))

fmt_k <- function(x) paste0("$", round(x / 1000), "k")
leg <- legend_bivariate("purple-green", classes = cty$bi,
                        style = "diamond", ends = FALSE, text_size = 8,
                        xlab = "Median income", ylab = "% with a degree",
                        labels = function(x) ifelse(x > 1000, fmt_k(x), paste0(round(x), "%")),
                        background = alpha("white", 0.9))

inset_legend(bimap, leg, position = "topleft", width = 0.32)
```

Dark teal on this map is "high income *and* many graduates": the suburbs of
Boston, New York and Philadelphia, 52 counties. Pale gray is the opposite
corner, 55 counties of rural Pennsylvania, upstate New York and northern Maine.
The two off-diagonal corners are nearly empty — two counties are high-income
with few graduates (Salem, NJ and Adams, PA), and one is low-income with many
(Windham, VT) — and that near-emptiness *is* the finding: in this region income
and education move together, and the map is a map of the exceptions. They sit
in the in-between cells: the mid-income, high-education college counties
(Tompkins, NY, home of Cornell, is one) in light green, and the
higher-income, lower-education commuter counties in light purple. That is
exactly what a single-variable map cannot show.

`counts = TRUE` writes the number of counties in every cell of the legend, and
an empty or nearly empty cell is the first thing to look for:

```{r}
#| label: bi-counts
#| fig-height: 3
legend_bivariate("purple-green", classes = cty$bi, counts = TRUE,
                 xlab = "Income", ylab = "% degree", ends = FALSE,
                 labels = function(x) ifelse(x > 1000, fmt_k(x), paste0(round(x), "%")))
```

### Legend layouts

Two layouts. `style = "square"` has an arrowed axis on each side and reads like
a chart. `style = "diamond"` is the square rotated 45°, both-low at the bottom
and both-high at the top; values run along the two lower edges, or
`corner_labels` puts a short phrase at each corner and drops the numbers
altogether. The corner-phrase version is the most readable for a general
audience, because it says what a color *means* rather than what the numbers
are.

```{r}
#| label: bi-legends
#| fig-height: 3
wrap_plots(
  legend_bivariate("blue-red", classes = cty$bi, xlab = "Income", ylab = "% degree",
                   ends = FALSE, text_size = 9,
                   labels = function(x) ifelse(x > 1000, fmt_k(x), paste0(round(x), "%"))),
  legend_bivariate("blue-red", 4, style = "diamond",
                   xlab = "% Black", ylab = "% Hispanic",
                   breaks_x = c(0, 5, 20, 50, 95), breaks_y = c(0, 5, 20, 50, 95),
                   labels = label_map(suffix = "%"), text_size = 9),
  legend_bivariate("blue-yellow", 3, style = "diamond", text_size = 8,
                   corner_labels = c("Low income\nfew graduates",
                                     "High income\nfew graduates",
                                     "Low income\nmany graduates",
                                     "High income\nmany graduates")),
  nrow = 1
)
```

## Project defaults: consistency is part of communication

When several maps belong to the same report, article, or dashboard, repeated
visual conventions help readers learn the design once and carry that knowledge
from map to map. If every sequential map should use one palette family and
every diverging map another, set those defaults once rather than rebuilding
them manually.
`ggcarto_palettes()` sets what the package reaches for when `palette` is not
given; on ggplot2 4.0 and later, `theme_palettes()` pushes the same choices
into ggplot2's own default scales so layers you have not styled match the ones
you have.

```{r}
#| label: defaults
#| fig-height: 5
old <- ggcarto_palettes(seq = "hcl::Batlow", div = "brewer::BrBG", cat = "brewer::Dark2")
ne_map(title = "No palette argument: uses the project default") +
  scale_fill_intervals(style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", digits = 1, suffix = "%"))
ggcarto_palettes(seq = old$seq, div = old$div, cat = old$cat)   # restore
```

## How ggcarto fits into the R mapping ecosystem

ggcarto is not meant to replace ggplot2, sf, classInt, tmap, or the major
palette packages. Its role is narrower: connect their strongest ideas inside a
regular ggplot2 workflow, while making the cartographic decisions visible
rather than burying them in scale defaults.

| Tool | What it does well | What it does not do |
|---|---|---|
| **ggplot2** `scale_fill_binned()`, `scale_fill_fermenter()`, `scale_fill_steps()` [@wickham2016] | Binned scales with a stepped color bar | Breaks and function limits come from the *limits*, so every data-driven classification silently becomes equal intervals; no interval labels; out-of-bounds values are dropped, not squished; no midpoint anchoring for binned scales |
| **scales** | Breaks and labels for charts (`breaks_pretty()`, `label_dollar()`) | No cartographic classification, no range labels |
| **classInt** [@classint] | Every classification algorithm, the reference implementation | Only computes the numbers; you still cut the data, build a manual scale and write the legend yourself; samples above 3,000 values |
| **tmap** [@tennekes2018] | Complete thematic mapping with classification, legends, layout | Its own grammar, not ggplot2; you cannot mix it with ggplot2 layers, themes, facets or patchwork |
| **biscale** [@biscale] | Bivariate maps in ggplot2, with Stevens's palettes | Bivariate only; its own break styles and palette names |
| **RColorBrewer, viridis, cols4all, paletteer, rcartocolor, scico** | Palettes | Palettes only, each with its own syntax |
| **colorspace** [@zeileis2020] | Color science: HCL, color-vision simulation, palette assessment | Not about maps or scales |
| **sf, ggspatial** | Geometry, projections, scale bars, basemaps | Nothing about color scales |
| **mapsf, cartography** | Thematic maps in base graphics | Not ggplot2 |

ggcarto is the layer that connects these inside ordinary ggplot2: it fixes the
binned-scale trap so classInt's algorithms actually work in a ggplot2 scale;
it reads palettes from every source above through one syntax; it adds the
map-shaped defaults (squish, midpoint, NA key, range labels); it makes the
mapping type a single argument, the way tmap does; it does bivariate maps with
the same break styles and palette syntax as everything else; and — the part
this version adds — it shows its working, so the classification, the class
count and the palette can each be inspected, defended and diagnosed.

What it deliberately does not do: geometry (use sf), projections and basemaps
(use sf and ggspatial), interactivity (use tmap or leaflet), or its own
palettes (use the ones that have been tested).

## The workflow in practice

The individual functions matter less than the order in which you use them. A
reliable workflow for a new choropleth is:

1. **Start with the question.** Decide what comparison the map should make
   easy: high versus low, above versus below a benchmark, top versus bottom of
   the distribution, change over time, or the relationship between two
   variables.
2. **Inspect the distribution.** Look for skew, gaps, outliers, repeated values,
   and missingness before choosing a classification method.
3. **Choose the representation deliberately.** Decide whether the variable
   should remain continuous, be classified, be shown by rank, or be paired with
   another variable. If you classify it, choose a method and class count that
   serve the question rather than simply accepting a default.
4. **Make the legend tell the same story as the map.** Use a palette whose
   visual logic matches the data, meaningful labels, an explicit midpoint when
   needed, and a separate treatment for missing values.
5. **Diagnose the finished map.** Check the actual class counts, limits,
   out-of-bounds values, palette behavior, and other choices after ggplot2 has
   trained the scale.

That sequence is the larger idea behind ggcarto. The package is useful not
because it automates cartography, but because it makes consequential decisions
**visible, inspectable, and reproducible**.

## Function reference, in one place

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `scale_fill_map()` / `scale_colour_map()` | The engine; `type` picks the mapping |
| `scale_fill_intervals()`, `_cont()`, `_cat()`, `_ord()`, `_rank()` | Same engine with `type` fixed |
| `class_guide()` | Suggest a number of classes, with the reasons and the metrics |
| `class_summary()` | The classes as a table: bounds, labels, counts |
| `plot_breaks()`, `compare_breaks()` | The breaks on the histogram, one method or several |
| `diagnose_map()`, `diagnose_scale()` | The decisions inside a finished scale, with warnings |
| `check_palette()`, `plot_palette()` | Lightness, distinguishability, color-vision simulation |
| `breaks_fisher(n)`, `breaks_quantile(n)`, `breaks_sd()`, `breaks_headtails()`, ... | Break functions; usable in any ggplot2 binned scale |
| `compute_breaks(x, style, n)` | The numbers, outside ggplot2; exact and reproducible |
| `map_styles()`, `map_styles_info()` | Which styles exist and what they do |
| `as_palette()`, `map_palettes()`, `show_palette()`, `palette_sources()` | Palette access |
| `label_map()` | Legend labels: ranges, open ends, `$`, `%`, thousands |
| `trim_limits()`, `symmetric_limits()` | Data-driven limits |
| `na_key()` | A "No data" legend key for interval and continuous scales |
| `classify_bivariate()`, `scale_fill_bivariate()`, `bivariate_palette()` | Bivariate classes and colors, with per-variable styles and transforms |
| `legend_bivariate()`, `inset_legend()` | The grid legend and where to put it |
| `ggcarto_palettes()`, `theme_palettes()` | Project-wide defaults |
| `theme_ggcarto()`, `guide_map()`, `ggcarto_colours()` | The map theme used here, a legend guide sized for it, and its colors |
| `bivariate_palettes()`, `plot_bivariate_palettes()` | The bivariate presets, listed and drawn |
| `northeast_counties` | The data used here |

The companion article *What a good choropleth has, and how ggcarto measures
it* (`vignette("good-maps")`) goes through every metric these functions
print and the design convention behind it.

## Recipes

```{r}
#| label: recipes
#| eval: false
# The workflow
class_guide(cty$x, "fisher")                  # inspect and choose
class_summary(cty$x, "fisher", 5)             # classify
plot_breaks(cty$x, "fisher", 5)
p <- ggplot(cty) + geom_sf(aes(fill = x)) +   # map
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "fisher", 5, range = c(0.15, 1),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", open = TRUE),
                       na.value = "grey85") +
  na_key("No data")
diagnose_map(p)                               # diagnose

# Money
scale_fill_intervals("hcl::Batlow", style = "quantile", n = 5,
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                        big.mark = ",", digits = 0))

# A rate, diverging around the regional figure
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", reverse = TRUE, n = 6, midpoint = 4.6,
                     limits = symmetric_limits(4.6),
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%", digits = 1))

# Counts: integer breaks, "0 to 4" labels, a policy threshold that means it
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "quantile", n = 5, as_count = TRUE)
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 20, 100), closure = "left",
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", open = TRUE))

# Counts with a long tail
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "headtails",
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", big.mark = ","))

# Same breaks on every map in a series
brks <- c(0, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10)
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", breaks = brks,
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%", open = TRUE))

# Rank-based color: robust to skew and extreme values
scale_fill_rank("brewer::YlGnBu")

# Two variables, one of them on a log scale
cty$cls <- classify_bivariate(cty$income, cty$degree, n = 3, trans_x = "log10")
map + scale_fill_bivariate("purple-green")
inset_legend(map, legend_bivariate("purple-green", classes = cty$cls,
                                   style = "diamond", ends = FALSE,
                                   xlab = "Income", ylab = "% degree"))
```
